blocks.content: Most people learn SQL in two steps: SELECT, then GROUP BY. Then they hit their first real analytics problem — "show me each salesperson's rank inside their own region" — and GROUP BY cannot help them. It collapses rows. You need the individual rows and the group calculation at the same time. That is exactly the gap window functions fill. A window function performs a calculation across a set of rows related to the current row, without collapsing them into one. Once this idea clicks, leaderboards, running totals, and trend reports become straightforward. Here are the four patterns that cover most of what you will ever need.

blocks.text: 1. What a window function actually is

blocks.content: Every window function ends with an OVER(...) clause, and that clause is where the magic lives. PARTITION BY splits rows into groups — think of it as GROUP BY that does not destroy the rows. ORDER BY defines the order of rows inside each group. The difference in a nutshell: GROUP BY gives you one row per group; a window function attaches the group calculation to every single row.
Each employee keeps their own row, but now every row also carries the average salary of their department. Comparing a value to its own group is something GROUP BY simply cannot express.

Rankings are the classic use case: top three products per category, highest-paid employee per department. Three functions cover it. ROW_NUMBER gives every row a unique number, ties included. RANK gives tied rows the same number and skips the next one — two rows ranked 1, then 3. DENSE_RANK gives tied rows the same number without skipping — two rows ranked 1, then 2. Pick the wrong one and your "top 10" quietly returns eleven rows.

blocks.code:
SELECT product, category, revenue
FROM (
  SELECT product, category, revenue,
         RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY category ORDER BY revenue DESC) AS rnk
  FROM sales
) t
WHERE rnk <= 3;

blocks.content: Note the subquery: window functions are computed after WHERE, so you cannot filter on them directly. Wrap first, filter second.

Put ORDER BY inside OVER without a PARTITION BY, and the window becomes a sliding frame: each row looks at every row from the start up to and including itself. That one trick produces running totals, cumulative signups, and burn-down charts. SUM(amount) OVER (ORDER BY order_date) is the entire technique. Swap SUM for AVG and you get a cumulative average.

blocks.code:
SELECT order_date,
       SUM(amount) OVER (ORDER BY order_date) AS running_total,
       AVG(amount) OVER (ORDER BY order_date) AS running_avg
FROM orders;

blocks.content: The default frame is "everything from the partition start up to the current row" — you rarely need to write it explicitly, but knowing it is there saves you from surprises when results look off.

blocks.text: 4. LAG and LEAD: compare with neighboring rows

blocks.content: Want month-over-month growth? The previous row's value is one function call away. LAG looks backward, LEAD looks forward. No self-joins, no date arithmetic, no correlated subqueries.

blocks.code:
WITH monthly AS (
  SELECT month, SUM(revenue) AS revenue
  FROM sales
  GROUP BY month
),
with_prev AS (
  SELECT month, revenue,
         LAG(revenue) OVER (ORDER BY month) AS prev_revenue
  FROM monthly
)
SELECT month, revenue, prev_revenue,
       ROUND(100.0 * (revenue - prev_revenue)
             / NULLIF(prev_revenue, 0), 1) AS pct_change
FROM with_prev;

blocks.content: NULLIF guards the division: on the first month, LAG returns NULL, and dividing by NULL would just propagate it — NULLIF keeps the math honest if a zero ever appears instead.

First: using a window function in WHERE. The WHERE clause runs before windows are computed, so the query fails or misbehaves. Wrap it in a subquery or CTE, as in the top-three example above. Second: forgetting PARTITION BY. Without it, the whole table becomes one group — your "per-region rank" silently becomes a global rank, and nobody notices until a stakeholder does. Third: LAG or LEAD without ORDER BY. Without an order, "previous row" is meaningless, and the database is free to hand you rows in any order it likes. The rule of thumb: a window function without ORDER BY is a bug waiting to happen — unless you genuinely want a whole-partition aggregate.

blocks.text: GROUP BY answers "how much per group". Window functions answer "how does this row compare to its group" — and that second question is where real analysis lives.

excerpt: GROUP BY collapses rows — window functions don't. Learn the four patterns (ranking, running totals, LAG/LEAD, plus the mistakes to avoid) that turn basic SQL into real analysis.
title: SQL Window Functions: The One Concept That Separates Beginners from Analysts
